papers.title: Mitophagy in neurodegeneration: crosstalk between PRKN/parkin-dependent and PRKN-independent pathways.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitochondria are cleared from cells through mitophagy, focusing on two main routes: one that depends on the PRKN/parkin protein and one that doesn't. It discusses how these pathways interact and overlap rather than working in isolation, and how their disruption is linked to neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's disease. The review likely synthesizes molecular mechanisms, key regulatory proteins, and disease-relevant crosstalk points between these pathways.
papers.why: Understanding both PRKN-dependent and PRKN-independent mitophagy mechanisms is essential for interpreting mito-QC/auto-QC reporter data across neuronal subtypes, since basal mitophagy in the ageing brain may rely on distinct or overlapping pathways not captured by parkin-centric models alone.

papers.title: Methyltransferase METTL1 Upregulates USF2 in a m7G-Dependent Manner to Accelerate Septic Cardiomyopathy by Inactivating PINK1/Parkin-Mediated Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the RNA-modifying enzyme METTL1 promotes septic cardiomyopathy, a heart dysfunction caused by sepsis. METTL1 adds m7G methylation marks that increase levels of the transcription factor USF2. This USF2 upregulation suppresses PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, impairing the heart's ability to clear damaged mitochondria and worsening cardiac injury.
papers.why: Although focused on sepsis rather than ageing, this paper offers mechanistic insight into PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy regulation in cardiac tissue, relevant to the mito-QC reporter work on physiological mitophagy in the heart.

papers.title: Exercise alleviates neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in aged mice via hepatic FGF21-driven microglial mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study shows that exercise in aged mice boosts hepatic secretion of FGF21, a liver-derived hormone. Circulating FGF21 then acts on microglia in the brain to enhance their mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria. This mitophagy-driven microglial rejuvenation reduces neuroinflammation and improves cognitive function in the aged mice.
papers.why: This paper links a systemic, organ-to-brain signaling axis with mitophagy as a driver of neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in aging, offering a physiological mitophagy model relevant to the age-related mitochondrial quality control mechanisms central to this project.

papers.title: Metformin Ameliorates Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction via p53/Parkin-Mediated Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study looks at whether the diabetes drug metformin can improve memory and thinking problems that occur in diabetes. The researchers propose that metformin works by boosting mitophagy, the process that clears out damaged mitochondria, through a p53/Parkin signaling pathway. They likely used a diabetic animal model to test cognitive outcomes alongside markers of mitochondrial quality control in brain tissue.
papers.why: This is relevant because it links a druggable pathway to p53/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in the brain, offering a potential physiological or pharmacological perturbation model to compare against baseline mito-QC reporter activity in neurons during ageing or metabolic stress.
papers.figure: The figure showing mitophagy markers (e.g., Parkin, LC3, PINK1) and mitochondrial morphology/quantity in brain neurons (hippocampus) with and without metformin treatment in diabetic vs control animals.

papers.title: Interplay between RNA m<sup>6</sup>A modification and transglutaminase 2 inhibitor effects on mitophagy dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper explores how RNA m6A methylation and a transglutaminase 2 (TG2) inhibitor interact to influence mitophagy defects in Alzheimer's disease. It likely proposes that TG2 inhibition can modulate m6A-marked transcripts involved in mitochondrial quality control, potentially restoring proper clearance of damaged mitochondria. The abstract suggests a mechanistic link between an RNA modification pathway and a druggable enzyme target as a way to correct impaired mitophagy in AD models.
papers.why: Understanding how RNA modifications and enzymatic regulators like TG2 converge on mitophagy dysfunction could inform how physiological mito-QC pathways are disrupted in neurodegeneration, offering mechanistic context for interpreting mito-QC reporter data in ageing neurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing co-localization of mitophagy markers (e.g., mito-QC-like reporters or LC3/mitochondria) with m6A-modified transcripts or TG2 activity in neurons treated with the TG2 inhibitor versus controls.

papers.title: Naringin reduces mitochondrial fragmentation and excessive mitophagy in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury via the S-nitrosylated Dynamin-related protein 1 (SNO-DRP1) / Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) / Mitochondrial Calcium Uniporter (MCU) pathway.
papers.summary: This study looks at how the natural compound naringin protects brain cells during stroke-like injury (ischemia-reperfusion). It shows that naringin blocks a chain of molecular events—S-nitrosylation of DRP1, followed by LRRK2 and MCU signaling—that normally causes mitochondria to fragment excessively and undergo too much mitophagy (self-destruction). By interrupting this pathway, naringin helps preserve mitochondrial health and reduces brain injury after ischemia-reperfusion.
papers.why: Although this is a pharmacological/disease-injury study rather than physiological ageing research, it identifies molecular regulators (DRP1/LRRK2/MCU-driven excessive mitophagy) that could inform mechanistic interpretation of mito-QC reporter changes seen in neurons under stress or ageing.
papers.figure: Figure showing quantification of mitochondrial fragmentation and mitophagy markers (e.g., mito-QC or LC3/mitochondrial colocalization) in neurons treated with naringin versus control after ischemia-reperfusion.

papers.title: High-Intensity Interval Training Ameliorates Oxidative Stress and Mitophagy in Heart Tissue of Healthy Rats Following the Combination Use of Methylphenidate and Ethanol.
papers.summary: This study looked at whether high-intensity interval training (HIIT) could protect the heart from oxidative stress and mitophagy changes caused by combined methylphenidate and ethanol use in healthy rats. The researchers found that exercise training reduced oxidative damage markers and altered mitophagy-related signaling in heart tissue compared to sedentary drug-exposed animals. The abstract suggests HIIT has a protective effect against drug-induced cardiac stress, likely by modulating mitochondrial quality control pathways.
papers.why: This paper touches on mitophagy in heart tissue using a pharmacological/exercise intervention model, which is tangentially relevant as a peripheral, non-neuronal, non-reporter-based example of mitochondrial quality control regulation but is otherwise disconnected from the core neuronal/spatial transcriptomics focus of the profile.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture mitigates cognitive impairment caused by CPB by facilitating PINK1-dependent mitophagy and synaptic plasticity.
papers.summary: This paper investigates whether electroacupuncture can reduce cognitive problems caused by cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) surgery, a procedure known to sometimes impair brain function afterward. The researchers propose that electroacupuncture works by boosting PINK1-dependent mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria from cells. They also suggest this treatment helps preserve synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or weaken connections between neurons, which is essential for learning and memory.
papers.why: This work connects to the profile's interest in PINK1-dependent mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons, though it applies these mechanisms in a surgical/injury context rather than physiological ageing.
papers.figure: A figure showing PINK1/mitophagy marker expression alongside synaptic plasticity measures (e.g., LTP or dendritic spine density) in electroacupuncture-treated versus control CPB animals would be most informative.
